claim: Aging is accompanied by disrupted information flow, resulting from accumulation of molecular mistakes.
source: Aging is accompanied by disrupted information flow, resulting from accumulation of molecular mistakes.
evidence: This is a statement in the abstract that draws from established scientific understanding of aging processes.

claim: Molecular mistakes ultimately give rise to debilitating disorders including skeletal muscle wasting, or sarcopenia.
source: These mistakes ultimately give rise to debilitating disorders including skeletal muscle wasting, or sarcopenia.
evidence: This statement is based on established knowledge linking molecular changes to sarcopenia.

claim: Escalating network entropy reached an inflection point at old age.
source: Escalating network entropy reached an inflection point at old age, while structural and functional alterations progressed into oldest-old age.
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in the manuscript showing entropy calculations across age groups.

claim: Structural and functional alterations progressed into oldest-old age.
source: Escalating network entropy reached an inflection point at old age, while structural and functional alterations progressed into oldest-old age.
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements of muscle structure and function across age groups.

claim: Klotho overexpression modulated genes representing all hallmarks of aging in old and oldest-old mice.
source: Klotho overexpression modulated genes representing all hallmarks of aging in old and oldest-old mice, but pathway enrichment revealed directions of changes were, for many genes, age-dependent.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data analysis showing differential gene expression in response to Klotho treatment.

claim: Pathway enrichment revealed directions of changes were, for many genes, age-dependent.
source: Klotho overexpression modulated genes representing all hallmarks of aging in old and oldest-old mice, but pathway enrichment revealed directions of changes were, for many genes, age-dependent.
evidence: This is supported by pathway analysis of RNA-seq data showing opposite responses in old versus oldest-old mice.

claim: Klotho improved strength in old mice.
source: Klotho improved strength in old mice, but failed to induce benefits beyond the entropic tipping point.
evidence: This is supported by functional testing data showing improved muscle force production in old mice treated with AAV-Klotho.

claim: Klotho failed to induce benefits beyond the entropic tipping point.
source: Klotho improved strength in old mice, but failed to induce benefits beyond the entropic tipping point.
evidence: This is supported by functional testing data showing no improvement in oldest-old mice treated with AAV-Klotho.

claim: López-Otín et al. described nine 'Hallmarks of Aging'.
source: With the goal of conceptualizing common molecular and cellular mechanisms that underlie the effect of time's arrow on mammalian tissue health, López-Otín et al. described nine 'Hallmarks of Aging' (López-Otín et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the López-Otín et al. 2013 publication.

claim: The nine hallmarks of aging are: epigenetic alterations, cellular senescence, altered intercellular communication, telomere attrition, nutrient sensing deregulation, mitochondrial dysfunction, stem cell exhaustion, loss of proteostasis, and genomic instability.
source: These hallmarks are: epigenetic alterations, cellular senescence, altered intercellular communication, telomere attrition, nutrient sensing deregulation, mitochondrial dysfunction, stem cell exhaustion, loss of proteostasis, and genomic instability.
evidence: This is a direct statement citing the established hallmarks from López-Otín et al.

claim: A criterion in the identification of hallmarks of aging was that aggravation or attenuation of the biological process results in an accelerated aging or more youthful phenotype, respectively.
source: A criterion in the identification of these hallmarks was that aggravation or attenuation of the biological process results in an accelerated aging or more youthful phenotype, respectively.
evidence: This is based on the criteria established by López-Otín et al. for defining hallmarks of aging.

claim: Numerous longitudinal aging studies have positively associated skeletal muscle health with healthspan and longevity.
source: Numerous longitudinal aging studies have positively associated skeletal muscle health with healthspan and longevity, and skeletal muscle strength has even been shown to be a reliable predictor of biological age and mortality (Bell et al., 2019; Voisin et al., 2020; Metter et al., 2002; Frontera et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published studies.

claim: Skeletal muscle strength has been shown to be a reliable predictor of biological age and mortality.
source: Numerous longitudinal aging studies have positively associated skeletal muscle health with healthspan and longevity, and skeletal muscle strength has even been shown to be a reliable predictor of biological age and mortality (Bell et al., 2019; Voisin et al., 2020; Metter et al., 2002; Frontera et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bell et al., 2019; Voisin et al., 2020; Metter et al., 2002; Frontera et al., 2000.

claim: An age-related loss of skeletal muscle mass and function (i.e., sarcopenia) is associated with loss of mobility and increased fall risk.
source: Furthermore, an age-related loss of skeletal muscle mass and function (i.e., sarcopenia) is associated with loss of mobility and increased fall risk (Kinney, 2004; Landi et al., 2012; Imagama et al., 2011; Goodpaster et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kinney, 2004; Landi et al., 2012; Imagama et al., 2011; Goodpaster et al., 2006.

claim: Tissue-level features of sarcopenia include a decreased myofiber size, increased intramuscular fat accumulation, a preferential atrophy of type II (fast-twitch) muscle fibers, and compromised function.
source: Tissue-level features of sarcopenia have been described extensively, and include a decreased myofiber size, increased intramuscular fat accumulation, a preferential atrophy of type II (fast-twitch) muscle fibers, and compromised function (Doherty, 2003; Morley et al., 2014; Miljkovic et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Doherty, 2003; Morley et al., 2014; Miljkovic et al., 2015.

claim: Our understanding of the cellular mechanisms underlying sarcopenia is still lacking.
source: However, our understanding of the cellular mechanisms underlying sarcopenia is still lacking, a shortcoming that has hindered the development of targeted and specific interventions (Marzetti et al., 2017; Dhillon and Hasni, 2017; Woo, 2017; Wang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Marzetti et al., 2017; Dhillon and Hasni, 2017; Woo, 2017; Wang et al., 2019.

claim: Currently, approaches to the treatment and prevention of sarcopenia largely focus on the prescription of physical activity and dietary modifications.
source: Currently, approaches to the treatment and prevention of sarcopenia largely focus on the prescription of physical activity and dietary modifications, strategies that have shown moderate success (Morley, 2018; Waters et al., 2010; Taaffe, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Morley, 2018; Waters et al., 2010; Taaffe, 2006.

claim: Physical activity and dietary modifications have shown moderate success in treating sarcopenia.
source: Currently, approaches to the treatment and prevention of sarcopenia largely focus on the prescription of physical activity and dietary modifications, strategies that have shown moderate success (Morley, 2018; Waters et al., 2010; Taaffe, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Morley, 2018; Waters et al., 2010; Taaffe, 2006.

claim: Proven pharmacological interventions for sarcopenia do not exist.
source: Furthermore, proven pharmacological interventions for sarcopenia do not exist, although drugs such as vitamin D, insulin-like growth factors, testosterone, cetylpyridinium chloride (CPC2), as well as monoclonal antibody treatments have entered advanced clinical trials (Woo, 2017; Drescher et al., 2016; Rolland et al., 2011; Becker et al., 2015; Bauer et al., 2015; https://clinicaltrials.gov/ct2/show/NCT01963598, https://clinicaltrials.gov/ct2/show/NCT02333331, https://clinicaltrials.gov/ct2/show/NCT02575235).
evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical trials and review articles.

claim: Drugs such as vitamin D, insulin-like growth factors, testosterone, cetylpyridinium chloride (CPC2), as well as monoclonal antibody treatments have entered advanced clinical trials for sarcopenia.
source: Furthermore, proven pharmacological interventions for sarcopenia do not exist, although drugs such as vitamin D, insulin-like growth factors, testosterone, cetylpyridinium chloride (CPC2), as well as monoclonal antibody treatments have entered advanced clinical trials (Woo, 2017; Drescher et al., 2016; Rolland et al., 2011; Becker et al., 2015; Bauer et al., 2015; https://clinicaltrials.gov/ct2/show/NCT01963598, https://clinicaltrials.gov/ct2/show/NCT02333331, https://clinicaltrials.gov/ct2/show/NCT02575235).
evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical trials and review articles.

claim: Many of the drugs currently being tested for sarcopenia also act on pathways associated with the longevity protein, α-Klotho (Klotho).
source: Interestingly, many of the drugs currently being tested also act on pathways associated with the longevity protein, α-Klotho (Klotho).
evidence: This is an inference based on the pathways targeted by the drugs mentioned and known Klotho signaling pathways.

claim: Klotho is best known for its role in delaying age-related pathologies in various organ systems, including skeletal muscle.
source: Klotho is best known for its role in delaying age-related pathologies in various organ systems, including skeletal muscle (Kurosu et al., 2005; Kuro-o et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kurosu et al., 2005; Kuro-o et al., 1997.

claim: The pro-longevity effects of Klotho have been partially attributed to modulation of fibroblast growth factor 23 (FGF23), Wnt, and mTOR pathways.
source: The pro-longevity effects of Klotho have been partially attributed to modulation of fibroblast growth factor 23 (FGF23), Wnt, and mTOR pathways (Hu et al., 2013; Liu et al., 2007; Zhao et al., 2015), several of which have also been a targets in sarcopenia research (Woo, 2017; Becker et al., 2015; Yoshida et al., 2019; D'Antona and Nisoli, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hu et al., 2013; Liu et al., 2007; Zhao et al., 2015.

claim: FGF23, Wnt, and mTOR pathways have been targets in sarcopenia research.
source: The pro-longevity effects of Klotho have been partially attributed to modulation of fibroblast growth factor 23 (FGF23), Wnt, and mTOR pathways (Hu et al., 2013; Liu et al., 2007; Zhao et al., 2015), several of which have also been a targets in sarcopenia research (Woo, 2017; Becker et al., 2015; Yoshida et al., 2019; D'Antona and Nisoli, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Woo, 2017; Becker et al., 2015; Yoshida et al., 2019; D'Antona and Nisoli, 2010.

claim: With age, circulating Klotho levels gradually decline.
source: With age, circulating Klotho levels gradually decline, and epidemiological studies have revealed that decreased circulating Klotho levels are associated with an accelerated loss of skeletal muscle mass and strength (Yamazaki et al., 2010; Semba et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Yamazaki et al., 2010; Semba et al., 2016.

claim: Epidemiological studies have revealed that decreased circulating Klotho levels are associated with an accelerated loss of skeletal muscle mass and strength.
source: With age, circulating Klotho levels gradually decline, and epidemiological studies have revealed that decreased circulating Klotho levels are associated with an accelerated loss of skeletal muscle mass and strength (Yamazaki et al., 2010; Semba et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Yamazaki et al., 2010; Semba et al., 2016.

claim: Mice deficient for Klotho display significant muscle wasting.
source: Similarly, mice deficient for Klotho display significant muscle wasting, which is hypothesized to be caused by increased mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (ROS) (Sahu et al., 2018; Phelps et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Sahu et al., 2018; Phelps et al., 2013.

claim: Muscle wasting in Klotho-deficient mice is hypothesized to be caused by increased mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (ROS).
source: Similarly, mice deficient for Klotho display significant muscle wasting, which is hypothesized to be caused by increased mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (ROS) (Sahu et al., 2018; Phelps et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Sahu et al., 2018; Phelps et al., 2013.

claim: Mitochondrial accumulation of ROS leads to a decline in muscle mass and decreased regenerative potential.
source: These findings are consistent with the observation that mitochondrial accumulation of ROS leads to a decline in muscle mass and decreased regenerative potential (Sahu et al., 2018; Leduc-Gaudet et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Sahu et al., 2018; Leduc-Gaudet et al., 2015.

claim: There is an unexplored mechanistic link between sarcopenia and a decline of Klotho with increasing age.
source: Taken together, these studies suggest an unexplored mechanistic link between sarcopenia and a decline of Klotho with increasing age.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited studies linking Klotho decline to muscle wasting.

claim: Network entropy increases from young (4–6 months) to old (21–24 months) mice, but then plateaus in the oldest-old mice (27–29 months).
source: We found that network entropy increases from young (4–6 months) to old (21–24 months) mice, but then plateaus in the oldest-old mice (27–29 months).
evidence: This is supported by data analysis of RNA-seq data showing entropy calculations.

claim: Old mice displayed a significant improvement in function with AAV-Kl treatment.
source: The impact of AAV-Kl was age-dependent, and whereas old mice displayed a significant improvement in function, AAV-Kl failed to induce a benefit in the oldest-old mice.
evidence: This is supported by functional testing data showing improved muscle performance in old mice.

claim: AAV-Kl failed to induce a benefit in the oldest-old mice.
source: The impact of AAV-Kl was age-dependent, and whereas old mice displayed a significant improvement in function, AAV-Kl failed to induce a benefit in the oldest-old mice.
evidence: This is supported by functional testing data showing no improvement in oldest-old mice.

claim: AAV-Kl regulated a multitude of genes associated with all hallmarks of aging.
source: Furthermore, AAV-Kl regulated a multitude of genes associated with all hallmarks of aging.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data analysis showing differential gene expression across all hallmarks.

claim: The direction of change in response to AAV-Kl treatment was, for many genes, dependent on the age of the host.
source: Unexpectedly, however, the direction of change in response to treatment was, for many genes, dependent on the age of the host.
evidence: This is supported by pathway analysis showing opposite responses in old versus oldest-old mice.

claim: Klotho enhances skeletal muscle structure and function at the early stages of sarcopenia.
source: Taken together, these results suggest Klotho enhances skeletal muscle structure and function at the early stages of sarcopenia, but the beneficial effects are lost after the entropic inflection point.
evidence: This is supported by functional and structural data in old mice treated with AAV-Klotho.

claim: The beneficial effects of Klotho are lost after the entropic inflection point.
source: Taken together, these results suggest Klotho enhances skeletal muscle structure and function at the early stages of sarcopenia, but the beneficial effects are lost after the entropic inflection point.
evidence: This is supported by the lack of functional improvement in oldest-old mice despite gene expression changes.

claim: A progressive decline in tibialis anterior (TA) wet weight (normalized to body weight) was observed over time for both males and females.
source: As expected, a progressive decline in tibialis anterior (TA) wet weight (normalized to body weight) was observed over time for both males and females, though the percent decrease at the oldest-old age was significantly greater in male mice (34%) when compared to females (17%; Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The percent decrease in TA weight at the oldest-old age was significantly greater in male mice (34%) when compared to females (17%).
source: As expected, a progressive decline in tibialis anterior (TA) wet weight (normalized to body weight) was observed over time for both males and females, though the percent decrease at the oldest-old age was significantly greater in male mice (34%) when compared to females (17%; Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: A decline in TA weight was concomitant with a decline in physiological cross-sectional area (CSA).
source: A decline in TA weight was concomitant with a decline in physiological cross-sectional area (CSA, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Bulk decreases in size and cross-sectional area were accompanied by a decrease in individual myofiber cross-sectional area for both sexes, though declines were greater in female mice.
source: Bulk decreases in size and cross-sectional area were accompanied by a decrease in individual myofiber cross-sectional area for both sexes, though declines were greater in female mice (Figure 1B,C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1B,C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The total number of muscle fibers did not change with age.
source: The total number of muscle fibers did not change with age (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: A decrease in the percentage of the more oxidative Type IIA and IIX muscle fibers was observed in the oldest-old, but not old, age group for both sexes.
source: A decrease in the percentage of the more oxidative Type IIA and IIX muscle fibers was observed in the oldest-old, but not old, age group for both sexes (Figure 1C,D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by fiber type analysis shown in Figure 1C,D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Changes in fiber type were accompanied by an increase in the percentage of the glycolytic Type IIB phenotype and a decrease in fiber area of all fiber types in oldest-old groups.
source: These changes were accompanied by an increase in the percentage of the glycolytic Type IIB phenotype and a decrease in fiber area of all fiber types in oldest-old groups (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–G).
evidence: This is supported by fiber type analysis shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–G.

claim: The loss of oxidative fiber types with age observed in this study is consistent with previous murine studies.
source: These results are consistent with a loss of oxidative fiber types with age observed in previous murine studies (Augusto et al., 2017; Giacomello et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Augusto et al., 2017; Giacomello et al., 2020.

claim: Increased intramuscular collagen deposition was observed in the oldest-old age groups of both sexes.
source: We also observed increased intramuscular collagen deposition in the oldest-old age groups of both sexes (Figure 1C,E, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by collagen staining data shown in Figure 1C,E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: There was no age-related increase in intermuscular lipid accumulation in either sex.
source: Unexpectedly, there was no age-related increase in intermuscular lipid accumulation in either sex (Figure 1C; Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by lipid staining data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1F.

claim: The lack of age-related increase in intermuscular lipid accumulation contrasts with clinical reports of muscle quality in older individuals.
source: This contrasts with clinical reports of muscle quality in older individuals (Doherty, 2003; Morley et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Doherty, 2003; Morley et al., 2014.

claim: A small increase in intramuscular lipid was observed only in old male mice.
source: We did observe a small increase in intramuscular lipid only in old male mice (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is supported by lipid staining data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Musk and Runx1 displayed increased expression in oldest-old mice.
source: Musk and Runx1 displayed increased expression in oldest-old mice, although sex differences could not be determined due to inadequate power (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Whole-body muscle strength, as measured by the four-limb hang test, gradually declined with increasing age for both male and female mice.
source: Whole-body muscle strength, as measured by the four-limb hang test, gradually declined with increasing age for both male and female mice (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by functional testing data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: In vivo contractile testing of the TA muscle revealed a significant decline in muscle strength only in the oldest-old mice, regardless of sex.
source: However, in vivo contractile testing of the TA muscle revealed a significant decline in muscle strength only in the oldest-old mice, regardless of sex (Figure 2B,C,D).
evidence: This is supported by contractile testing data shown in Figure 2B,C,D.

claim: Changes in temporal characteristics of the muscle contraction profile, including increased time to peak twitch contraction and half relaxation time, were most prominent in the oldest-old female group.
source: Changes in temporal characteristics of the muscle contraction profile, including increased time to peak twitch contraction and half relaxation time, were also most prominent in the oldest-old female group (Figure 2E,F).
evidence: This is supported by contractile testing data shown in Figure 2E,F.

claim: Temporal changes in muscle contraction are consistent with the decreased area of fast-twitch fiber phenotypes and coincide with clinical reports.
source: These temporal changes are consistent with the decreased area of fast-twitch fiber phenotypes and coincide with clinical reports (Miljkovic et al., 2015; Larsson et al., 1978; Lexell and Taylor, 1991).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Miljkovic et al., 2015; Larsson et al., 1978; Lexell and Taylor, 1991.

claim: Old mice display a mild sarcopenic profile and common features associated with clinical metrics of sarcopenia only become evident in oldest-old mice.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that old mice display a mild sarcopenic profile and that common features associated with clinical metrics of sarcopenia only become evident in oldest-old mice.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural and functional data presented.

claim: Principal Component Analysis (PCA) revealed distinct gene expression profiles according to age, with young muscle segregating from the old and oldest-old muscle profiles, the latter of which slightly overlapped.
source: Principal Component Analysis (PCA) revealed distinct gene expression profiles according to age, with young muscle segregating from the old and oldest-old muscle profiles, the latter of which slightly overlapped (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by PCA analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: PCA findings are consistent with previous transcriptomic studies of human skeletal muscle in which the bulk of gene expression changes occur between young and old age, after which time they plateau.
source: These findings are consistent with previous transcriptomic studies of human skeletal muscle in which the bulk of gene expression changes occur between young and old age, after which time they plateau (Cellerino and Ori, 2017; Byrne et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Cellerino and Ori, 2017; Byrne et al., 2019.

claim: Of the top 100 genes in PC2 that varied according to age, 59 out of 100 genes were associated with hallmarks of aging.
source: Of these, 59 out of 100 genes were associated with hallmarks of aging and, most prominently, genes associated with altered intercellular communication and nutrient-sensing deregulation.
evidence: This is supported by gene ontology analysis of PC2 genes.

claim: The top 100 genes for PC2 are most prominently associated with altered intercellular communication and nutrient-sensing deregulation.
source: Of these, 59 out of 100 genes were associated with hallmarks of aging and, most prominently, genes associated with altered intercellular communication and nutrient-sensing deregulation.
evidence: This is supported by gene ontology analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: Gene Ontology enrichment confirmed that the top 100 genes for PC2 are associated with cellular homeostasis, cellular structure, and intercellular communication.
source: Gene Ontology enrichment confirmed that the top 100 genes for PC2 are associated with cellular homeostasis, cellular structure, and intercellular communication (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is supported by gene ontology analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: The greatest increase in network entropy was observed between young and old groups, with little difference between the old and the oldest-old.
source: Consistent with PCA findings, but contrary to phenotypic changes, we observed the greatest increase in network entropy between young and old groups, with little difference between the old and the oldest-old (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by network entropy calculations shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Gene expression changes likely precede the observed functional deficits in oldest-old mice.
source: This suggests that gene expression changes likely precede the observed functional deficits in oldest-old mice (Figure 2).
evidence: This is an inference based on the entropy data and functional data.

claim: The same entropy trend emerged even when all genes were considered, suggesting that the subset of genes associated with the hallmarks of aging captures the overall tissue transcriptomic profile without loss of information.
source: The same entropy trend emerged even when all genes were considered, suggesting that the subset of genes associated with the hallmarks of aging captures the overall tissue transcriptomic profile without loss of information (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by network entropy calculations shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The increase in entropy between young and old muscles was driven by a relatively small pool of genes that displayed a large magnitude of change.
source: Furthermore, we found that the increase in entropy between young and old muscles was driven by a relatively small pool of genes that displayed a large magnitude of change (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by gene count distribution analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: There were many more DE genes when comparing old and oldest-old muscles, although the magnitudes of change were generally low.
source: In contrast, there were many more DE genes when comparing old and oldest-old muscles, although the magnitudes of change were generally low (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by gene count distribution analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: The data suggest a loss of specific changes and a broadening of gene expression alterations across the genome in the oldest-old age group.
source: This suggests a loss of specific changes and a broadening of gene expression alterations across the genome in the oldest-old age group.
evidence: This is an inference based on the gene expression data.

claim: In male mice, entropy continued to increase from old to oldest-old timepoints, unlike females.
source: Unlike females, we saw that entropy continued to increase from old to oldest-old timepoints (Figure 3—figure supplement 4A), which we found interesting considering that male mice showed less severe sarcopenic declines at the oldest-old age (Figures 1 and 2).
evidence: This is supported by network entropy calculations shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4A.

claim: Male mice showed less severe sarcopenic declines at the oldest-old age compared to females.
source: Unlike females, we saw that entropy continued to increase from old to oldest-old timepoints (Figure 3—figure supplement 4A), which we found interesting considering that male mice showed less severe sarcopenic declines at the oldest-old age (Figures 1 and 2).
evidence: This is supported by structural and functional data shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: In male mice, entropy was lowest at the middle-aged timepoint, then gradually increased.
source: Also interesting, entropy was lowest at the middle-aged timepoint, then gradually increased.
evidence: This is supported by network entropy calculations shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4A.

claim: In rats, entropy decreased from young to middle-age, after which time it increased into old age, consistent with the trend observed in male mice.
source: In rats, entropy decreased from young to middle-age, after which time it increased into old age, consistent with the aforementioned trend observed in male mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: This is supported by network entropy calculations shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4B.

claim: Entropy in humans decreased from young adulthood into the fourth decade of life, after which time it increased, reaching a tipping point in the sixth decade of life, then decreasing slightly.
source: Entropy in humans similarly decreased from young adulthood into the fourth decade of life, after which time it increased, reaching a tipping point in the sixth decade of life, then decreasing slightly (Figure 3—figure supplement 4C).
evidence: This is supported by network entropy calculations shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4C.

claim: The entropic nadir in humans coincides with the commonly observed onset of sarcopenic declines in the fourth decade of life.
source: It is interesting to note that the entropic nadir in humans coincides with the commonly observed onset of sarcopenic declines in the fourth decade of life (Walston, 2012; Yazar and Olgun Yazar, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Walston, 2012; Yazar and Olgun Yazar, 2019.

claim: All of the hallmarks of aging were similarly affected when considering changes between young and old mice and young and the oldest-old mice, although roughly twice as many genes changed in the oldest-old mice.
source: Unexpectedly, we found that all of the hallmarks were similarly affected when considering changes between young and old mice and young and the oldest-old mice, although roughly twice as many genes changed in the oldest-old mice (Figure 3F,G).
evidence: This is supported by differential gene expression analysis shown in Figure 3F,G.

claim: The finding that roughly twice as many genes changed in the oldest-old mice implies a dysregulation of the transcriptomic profile in the oldest-old mice.
source: This further implies a dysregulation of the transcriptomic profile in the oldest-old mice, a finding that is consistent with previous reports (Cellerino and Ori, 2017).
evidence: This is an inference based on the gene expression data and supported by citation to Cellerino and Ori, 2017.

claim: Circulating Klotho gradually declines with age in mice, consistent with human findings.
source: As a first step, we confirmed that circulating Klotho gradually declines with age in mice, consistent with human findings (Yamazaki et al., 2010; Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 4A and citation to Yamazaki et al., 2010.

claim: In both sexes, a stepwise increase in circulating fibroblast growth factor-23 (FGF23) was observed with age.
source: In both sexes, we also observed a stepwise increase in circulating fibroblast growth factor-23 (FGF23), a known co-factor for Klotho signaling and a key hormone in the regulation of mineral ions and vitamin D (Chen et al., 2018; Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: FGF23 is a known co-factor for Klotho signaling and a key hormone in the regulation of mineral ions and vitamin D.
source: In both sexes, we also observed a stepwise increase in circulating fibroblast growth factor-23 (FGF23), a known co-factor for Klotho signaling and a key hormone in the regulation of mineral ions and vitamin D (Chen et al., 2018; Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Chen et al., 2018.

claim: Circulating FGF23 levels in the oldest-old females clustered into two different groups, with approximately 40% of the population displaying very high levels compared to the more linearly increasing levels of the remaining mice.
source: It was interesting to note that circulating FGF23 levels in the oldest-old females clustered into two different groups, with approximately 40% of the population displaying very high levels compared to the more linearly increasing levels of the remaining mice.
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The variation in FGF23 levels may be a result of varied hormonal status across the cohort.
source: This variation may be a result of varied hormonal status across the cohort.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observed variation in FGF23 levels.

claim: 20–40% of female mice spontaneously regenerate follicles after menopause.
source: Although hormone levels were not measured here, it has previously been shown that 20–40% of female mice spontaneously regenerate follicles after menopause (Diaz Brinton, 2012), which is relevant given that estrogen levels have been shown to regulate circulating FGF23 in both rodents and humans (Ix et al., 2011; Saki et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Diaz Brinton, 2012.

claim: Estrogen levels have been shown to regulate circulating FGF23 in both rodents and humans.
source: Although hormone levels were not measured here, it has previously been shown that 20–40% of female mice spontaneously regenerate follicles after menopause (Diaz Brinton, 2012), which is relevant given that estrogen levels have been shown to regulate circulating FGF23 in both rodents and humans (Ix et al., 2011; Saki et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ix et al., 2011; Saki et al., 2020.

claim: Three weeks after AAV administration, qPCR confirmed that the vector was inserted into the genome in the liver and replicated.
source: Three weeks after administration, qPCR confirmed that the vector was inserted into the genome in the liver and replicated (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: MSD-ELISA conducted on serum confirmed a dose-dependent increase in circulating Klotho levels.
source: Meso Scale Discovery-Enzyme-linked Immune Sorbent Assay (MSD-ELISA) conducted on serum further confirmed a dose-dependent increase in circulating Klotho levels (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by MSD-ELISA data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Klotho transcript levels in the gastrocnemius muscles of old and oldest-old mice were unaffected by AAV-Kl administration, consistent with use of a liver-specific promoter.
source: Klotho transcript levels in the gastrocnemius muscles of old and oldest-old mice were unaffected by AAV-Kl administration, consistent with use of a liver-specific promoter (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The AAV expression of Klotho had no significant effects on non-fasting serum insulin, glucose, cholesterol, or other circulating lipids.
source: Lastly, the AAV expression of Klotho had no significant effects on non-fasting serum insulin, glucose, cholesterol, or other circulating lipids (Figure 4G,H,I; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by metabolite analysis data shown in Figure 4G,H,I and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: There was no difference in myofiber cross-sectional area in the injured TAs of animals treated with AAV-Kl when compared to control counterparts.
source: There was no difference in myofiber cross-sectional area in the injured TAs of animals treated with AAV-Kl when compared to control counterparts (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by histological analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Fibrosis was significantly decreased in the TAs of AAV-Kl-treated mice, as evidenced by decreased collagen deposition.
source: However, fibrosis was significantly decreased in the TAs of AAV-Kl-treated mice, as evidenced by decreased collagen deposition (Figure 5C,D,E).
evidence: This is supported by collagen staining data shown in Figure 5C,D,E.

claim: The decrease in fibrosis was concomitant with a decreased number of fibroadipogenic progenitor cells (FAPs) with AAV-Kl treatment.
source: This decrease in fibrosis was concomitant with a decreased number of fibroadipogenic progenitor cells (FAPs) with AAV-Kl treatment, as quantified by flow cytometry and following a previously published protocol (Yi and Rossi, 2011; Liu et al., 2015; Figure 5F).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: AAV-Kl administration significantly increased the percentage of healthy mitochondria in aged regenerating muscle.
source: Indeed, AAV-Kl administration significantly increased the percentage of healthy mitochondria in aged regenerating muscle (Figure 5G,H).
evidence: This is supported by TEM data shown in Figure 5G,H.

claim: Mice receiving AAV-Kl displayed increased specific twitch and maximum specific tetanic force production.
source: Structural improvements were consistent with functional outcomes, and mice receiving AAV-Kl also displayed increased specific twitch and maximum specific tetanic force production (Figure 5I,J).
evidence: This is supported by contractile testing data shown in Figure 5I,J.

claim: Resistance to a fatiguing protocol was not affected by AAV-Kl treatment.
source: Resistance to a fatiguing protocol was not affected by treatment, although force recovery following completion of the fatiguing protocol was significantly enhanced in mice treated with AAV-Kl (Figure 5K).
evidence: This is supported by contractile testing data shown in Figure 5K.

claim: Force recovery following completion of the fatiguing protocol was significantly enhanced in mice treated with AAV-Kl.
source: Resistance to a fatiguing protocol was not affected by treatment, although force recovery following completion of the fatiguing protocol was significantly enhanced in mice treated with AAV-Kl (Figure 5K).
evidence: This is supported by contractile testing data shown in Figure 5K.

claim: Whole-body strength improved almost twofold over 14 days for mice treated with AAV-Kl; control mice showed no improvement.
source: Additionally, whole-body strength improved almost twofold over 14 days for mice treated with AAV-Kl; control mice showed no improvement (Figure 5L).
evidence: This is supported by hang test data shown in Figure 5L.

claim: Systemically elevated Klotho levels enhance skeletal muscle regeneration, similar to a previous report using intraperitoneal injection of recombinant Klotho.
source: These results confirmed that systemically elevated Klotho levels enhance skeletal muscle regeneration, similar to a previous report using intraperitoneal injection of recombinant Klotho (Sahu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by the functional and structural data and citation to Sahu et al., 2018.

claim: Animals treated with AAV-Kl displayed no significant increase in muscle performance following an exercise-induced injury.
source: In vivo contractile testing performed 7 days after injury revealed that animals treated with AAV-Kl displayed no significant increase in muscle performance (Figure 5M).
evidence: This is supported by contractile testing data shown in Figure 5M.

claim: The dose of 3 × 10^8 vector genomes per mouse was chosen because it provided the greatest improvement in muscle strength in old mice.
source: This dose was chosen because it provided the greatest improvement in muscle strength, as determined over the course of a preliminary dose-testing study performed in old mice (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by dose-response data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Of the 51 old and oldest-old mice included, only 30 mice were included in final analyses due to incidental morbidity and mortality, with most of these losses occurring prior to randomization.
source: Of the 51 old and oldest-old mice included, only 30 mice were included in final analyses due to incidental morbidity and mortality, with most of these losses occurring prior to randomization (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by the animal inclusion flow chart shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Histological analysis of old muscles revealed no improvement in the muscle weight, myofiber cross-sectional area, fiber number, or percentage of type IIA/X fibers with AAV-Kl treatment.
source: Histological analysis of old muscles revealed no improvement in the muscle weight, myofiber cross-sectional area, fiber number, or percentage of type IIA/X fibers with AAV-Kl treatment (Figure 6C,D,E,F, Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by histological data shown in Figure 6C,D,E,F and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: There was no change in expression of denervation genes with Klotho treatment in old mice.
source: There was also no change in expression of the previously mentioned denervation genes with Klotho treatment (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Intramuscular lipid accumulation was significantly decreased following AAV-Kl treatment in old mice.
source: However, intramuscular lipid accumulation was significantly decreased following treatment (Figure 6C,G).
evidence: This is supported by lipid staining data shown in Figure 6C,G.

claim: Maximum specific force production improved by 17% in old female mice treated with AAV-Kl.
source: Specifically, maximum specific force production improved by 17% (Figure 6H), and whole-body endurance measured via four-limb hang test was 60% greater when compared to control counterparts (Figure 6I).
evidence: This is supported by contractile testing data shown in Figure 6H.

claim: Whole-body endurance measured via four-limb hang test was 60% greater in old mice treated with AAV-Kl when compared to control counterparts.
source: Specifically, maximum specific force production improved by 17% (Figure 6H), and whole-body endurance measured via four-limb hang test was 60% greater when compared to control counterparts (Figure 6I).
evidence: This is supported by hang test data shown in Figure 6I.

claim: Unlike old mice, there was no improvement in any of the metrics evaluated in oldest-old mice treated with AAV-Kl.
source: Unlike old mice, there was no improvement in any of the metrics evaluated (Figure 6C,J–O, Figure 6—figure supplement 1B,D).
evidence: This is supported by histological and functional data shown in Figure 6C,J–O and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B,D.

claim: AAV-Kl administration significantly increased overall lipid accumulation in oldest-old mice.
source: In fact, AAV-Kl administration significantly increased overall lipid accumulation (Figure 6C,M).
evidence: This is supported by lipid staining data shown in Figure 6C,M.

claim: Systemic upregulation of Klotho induces therapeutic benefits in old mice, but not in mice of more advanced age.
source: These findings suggest that systemic upregulation of Klotho induces therapeutic benefits in old mice, but not in mice of more advanced age.
evidence: This is an inference based on the functional and structural data in old versus oldest-old mice.

claim: When comparing age-matched control and AAV-Kl treatment groups, approximately three times more DE genes were observed in the oldest-old group treated with Klotho as compared to the old group.
source: When comparing age-matched control and AAV-Kl treatment groups, we observed approximately three times more DE genes in the oldest-old group treated with Klotho as compared to the old group (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by differential gene expression analysis shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Existing literature suggests that Klotho attenuates hallmarks associated with mitochondrial dysfunction, telomere attrition, and cellular senescence.
source: Existing literature suggests that Klotho attenuates hallmarks associated with mitochondrial dysfunction, telomere attrition, and cellular senescence (Sahu et al., 2018; Kuro-o, 2008; Ullah and Sun, 2019; Frenk and Houseley, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Sahu et al., 2018; Kuro-o, 2008; Ullah and Sun, 2019; Frenk and Houseley, 2018.

claim: AAV-Kl affected all the hallmarks of aging similarly.
source: However, we found that AAV-Kl affected all the hallmarks similarly (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by differential gene expression analysis shown in Figure 7B.

claim: DE genes responsive to Klotho therapy in old mice were associated with pathways related to inhibition of FGFR4/calcineurin/NFAT signaling.
source: DE genes responsive to Klotho therapy in old mice were associated with pathways related to inhibition of FGFR4/calcineurin/NFAT signaling.
evidence: This is supported by pathway enrichment analysis shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The findings are consistent with previous reports demonstrating that overexpression of Klotho reverts pathogenic FGF23 signaling to more normal tissue homeostasis.
source: These findings are consistent with previous reports demonstrating that overexpression of Klotho reverts pathogenic FGF23 signaling to more normal tissue homeostasis (Xiao et al., 2019; Ho and Bergwitz, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Xiao et al., 2019; Ho and Bergwitz, 2021.

claim: FGFR4/calcineurin/NFAT signaling did not rise to the top of gene expression changes in response to Klotho treatment in the oldest-old mice.
source: Intriguingly, however, FGFR4/calcineurin/NFAT signaling did not rise to the top of gene expression changes in response to Klotho treatment in the oldest-old mice (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is supported by pathway enrichment analysis shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Neither circulating FGF23 protein levels, nor FGF23 transcript levels, nor the transcript levels of FGF23 and Klotho primary interactors were affected by Klotho treatment in either age group.
source: Of note, neither circulating FGF23 protein levels, nor FGF23 transcript levels, nor the transcript levels of FGF23 and Klotho primary interactors were affected by Klotho treatment in either age group (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA and RNA-seq data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The data suggest that the gain in Klotho may revert pathogenic FGF23 signaling through FGFR4 in old, but not oldest-old, mice.
source: The data suggest that the gain in Klotho may revert pathogenic FGF23 signaling through FGFR4 in old, but not oldest-old, mice (Ho and Bergwitz, 2021).
evidence: This is an inference based on the pathway analysis and supported by citation to Ho and Bergwitz, 2021.

claim: Regulation of actin cytoskeleton, cGMP-PKG signaling pathway, and sphingolipid signaling pathway were among the top pathways in which the gene response to Klotho was opposed in the old versus oldest-old mice.
source: Regulation of actin cytoskeleton, cGMP-PKG signaling pathway, and sphingolipid signaling pathway were among the top pathways in which the gene response to Klotho was opposed in the old versus oldest-old mice (Figure 7D, Figure 7—figure supplement 2, Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by KEGG pathway enrichment analysis shown in Figure 7D, Figure 7—figure supplement 2, and Table 1.

claim: The reversal of sphingosine/ceramide signaling by Klotho may have facilitated the reduction of intramyocellular lipid accumulation observed in old animals.
source: Significantly, the reversal of sphingosine/ceramide signaling by Klotho may have facilitated the reduction of intramyocellular lipid accumulation observed in old animals (Figure 6C; Hamrick et al., 2016).
evidence: This is speculation based on the pathway analysis and supported by citation to Hamrick et al., 2016.

claim: The reversal of sphingosine/ceramide signaling was absent in the Klotho-treated oldest-old mice, suggesting that a dysfunctional metabolism prevails with extreme aging.
source: This reversal was absent in the Klotho-treated oldest-old mice, suggesting that a dysfunctional metabolism prevails with extreme aging.
evidence: This is an inference based on the pathway analysis and lipid accumulation data.

claim: Cytoskeletal regulation and calcium ion transport are sensitive to Klotho regulation in old mice.
source: Further scrutiny of the top three pathways for mechanisms of Klotho's action revealed cytoskeletal regulation and calcium ion transport as sensitive to Klotho regulation in old mice (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by pathway analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: Cytoskeletal regulation and calcium ion transport are tightly linked to pathogenic, non-canonical FGF23 signaling.
source: These are all tightly linked to pathogenic, non-canonical FGF23 signaling (Xiao et al., 2019; Ho and Bergwitz, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Xiao et al., 2019; Ho and Bergwitz, 2021.

claim: Klotho overexpression in the oldest-old mice disrupted pathways regulating cell structure, cell membrane integrity, and intercellular communication.
source: In contrast, Klotho overexpression in the oldest-old mice disrupted pathways regulating cell structure, cell membrane integrity, and intercellular communication, which is consistent with the observed decreased contractile capacity (Figure 6N).
evidence: This is supported by pathway analysis and functional data shown in Figure 6N.

claim: The disruption of pathways regulating cell structure, cell membrane integrity, and intercellular communication is consistent with the observed decreased contractile capacity in oldest-old mice.
source: In contrast, Klotho overexpression in the oldest-old mice disrupted pathways regulating cell structure, cell membrane integrity, and intercellular communication, which is consistent with the observed decreased contractile capacity (Figure 6N).
evidence: This is an inference based on the pathway analysis and functional data shown in Figure 6N.

claim: Intervention with AAV-Kl may be more effective in slowing the progression of sarcopenia at an earlier timepoint, rather than rescuing advanced pathology.
source: Taken together, the data presented here suggest that intervention with AAV-Kl may be more effective in slowing the progression of sarcopenia at an earlier timepoint, rather than rescuing advanced pathology, at which time the transcriptomic response to intervention appears to be more stochastic.
evidence: This is an inference based on the age-dependent responses to AAV-Kl treatment.

claim: At advanced pathology, the transcriptomic response to intervention appears to be more stochastic.
source: Taken together, the data presented here suggest that intervention with AAV-Kl may be more effective in slowing the progression of sarcopenia at an earlier timepoint, rather than rescuing advanced pathology, at which time the transcriptomic response to intervention appears to be more stochastic.
evidence: This is an inference based on the gene expression data in oldest-old mice.

claim: The onset of sarcopenia in mice over time and according to sex has not been well-documented.
source: The onset of sarcopenia in mice over time and according to sex has not been well-documented (Romanick et al., 2013; Argilés et al., 2015), as studies of sarcopenia in animal models often exclude the oldest-old cohort (Romanick et al., 2013; Uchitomi et al., 2019; van Dijk et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Romanick et al., 2013; Argilés et al., 2015; Uchitomi et al., 2019; van Dijk et al., 2017.

claim: Studies of sarcopenia in animal models often exclude the oldest-old cohort.
source: The onset of sarcopenia in mice over time and according to sex has not been well-documented (Romanick et al., 2013; Argilés et al., 2015), as studies of sarcopenia in animal models often exclude the oldest-old cohort (Romanick et al., 2013; Uchitomi et al., 2019; van Dijk et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Romanick et al., 2013; Uchitomi et al., 2019; van Dijk et al., 2017.

claim: Decreased muscle mass and function become prominent in the oldest-old group, whereas muscle declines in old mice are relatively modest.
source: We found that decreased muscle mass and function – two classical markers of sarcopenia – become prominent in the oldest-old group, whereas muscle declines in old mice are relatively modest.
evidence: This is supported by the structural and functional data presented in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: The onset of sarcopenia in mice appears to be sexually dimorphic, with females displaying slightly accelerated functional declines.
source: Additionally, the onset of sarcopenia in mice appears to be sexually dimorphic, with females displaying slightly accelerated functional declines.
evidence: This is supported by the structural and functional data presented in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: The findings are in agreement with one previous clinical report suggesting that sarcopenia progresses more rapidly in females.
source: These findings are in agreement with one previous clinical report suggesting that sarcopenia progresses more rapidly in females (Masanes et al., 2012), although other studies demonstrated minimal differences between males and females (Morley et al., 2014; Tay et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Masanes et al., 2012.

claim: Other studies demonstrated minimal differences between males and females in sarcopenia progression.
source: These findings are in agreement with one previous clinical report suggesting that sarcopenia progresses more rapidly in females (Masanes et al., 2012), although other studies demonstrated minimal differences between males and females (Morley et al., 2014; Tay et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Morley et al., 2014; Tay et al., 2015.

claim: Clinical studies performed in older adults have suggested that loss of muscle function is predominantly a result of a loss of muscle quality, as opposed to a loss of muscle mass.
source: Clinical studies performed in older adults have suggested that loss of muscle function is predominantly a result of a loss of muscle quality, as opposed to a loss of muscle mass (Goodpaster et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Goodpaster et al., 2006.

claim: In this study, age-related functional declines were not accompanied by a significant loss of muscle mass.
source: Likewise, in our study, age-related functional declines were not accompanied by a significant loss of muscle mass.
evidence: This is supported by the structural data presented in Figure 1.

claim: Muscle mass and myofiber area were, for the most part, preserved over time.
source: Instead, muscle mass and myofiber area were, for the most part, preserved over time.
evidence: This is supported by the structural data presented in Figure 1.

claim: Although muscle mass decreased by only approximately 10% between the old and oldest-old age groups, the accompanying decrease in peak force production was over two-fold greater.
source: Although muscle mass decreased by only approximately 10% between the old and oldest-old age groups, the accompanying decrease in peak force production was over two-fold greater.
evidence: This is supported by the structural and functional data presented in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Several transcriptional studies using functional enrichment of differentially expressed genes have reported that age-related changes play a key role in the progression of sarcopenia.
source: Several transcriptional studies using functional enrichment of differentially expressed genes have reported that age-related changes play a key role in the progression of sarcopenia (Shavlakadze et al., 2019; Barns et al., 2014; Zahn et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Shavlakadze et al., 2019; Barns et al., 2014; Zahn et al., 2006.

claim: Evaluation of the interconnectedness of the PPI interactome allows for a single, integrative metric to estimate the 'disorderliness' of the system.
source: Although an aging system is not necessarily closed (a now overturned criteria for an entropic system) (Hayflick, 2007; Samaras, 1974), evaluation of the interconnectedness of the PPI interactome allows for a single, integrative metric to estimate the 'disorderliness' of the system (Menichetti et al., 2015; Menichetti and Remondini, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Menichetti et al., 2015; Menichetti and Remondini, 2014.

claim: The PPI network allows visualization of the functional relationship between genes, an approach that has been used in several studies that explore the mechanism of complex diseases.
source: As such, the PPI network allows visualization of the functional relationship between genes, an approach that has been used in several studies that explore the mechanism of complex diseases (Zahn et al., 2006; Samaras, 1974; Shannon, 1948; Teschendorff and Enver, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Zahn et al., 2006; Samaras, 1974; Shannon, 1948; Teschendorff and Enver, 2017.

claim: Similar to a previous report using microarray gene data from human circulating T-lymphocytes, network entropy increased from young to old mice.
source: Similar to a previous report using microarray gene data from human circulating T-lymphocytes, we observed that network entropy increased from young to old mice (Menichetti et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Menichetti et al., 2015.

claim: The absolute magnitude of entropy change is small, comparable to entropy change estimates in the context of stem cell differentiation, cancer, and aging.
source: Comparable to entropy change estimates in the context of stem cell differentiation, cancer, and aging (Menichetti et al., 2015; Teschendorff and Enver, 2017; Kannan et al., 2020; Park et al., 2016; Conforte et al., 2019), the absolute magnitude of entropy change in our study is small.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Menichetti et al., 2015; Teschendorff and Enver, 2017; Kannan et al., 2020; Park et al., 2016; Conforte et al., 2019.

claim: The small percentage change in entropy captures the change in expression of a large number of genes (~7600 genes), each of which has the potential to elicit a cascade of downstream phenotypic changes.
source: However, this small percentage captures the change in expression of a large number of genes (~7600 genes), each of which has the potential to elicit a cascade of downstream phenotypic changes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the entropy calculations and the number of genes involved.

claim: From a physiological perspective, there is growing evidence that very small-scale mRNA changes can lead to extreme changes at the level of protein expression and cellular phenotype.
source: Indeed, from a physiological perspective, there is growing evidence that very small-scale mRNA changes can lead to extreme changes at the level of protein expression and cellular phenotype (Ruzycki et al., 2015; Cheng et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ruzycki et al., 2015; Cheng et al., 2016.

claim: In the context of cancer, a single base mutation led to extensive cell remodeling that extended well beyond the predicted downstream responses, a so-called 'butterfly effect'.
source: In the context of cancer, for example, a single base mutation led to extensive cell remodeling that extended well beyond the predicted downstream responses, a so-called 'butterfly effect' (Hart et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hart et al., 2015.

claim: Cells display a sensitive dependence to initial conditions (in this case, gene expression), and very small changes in transcriptional regulation and equilibrium may exert potent – perhaps even chaotic – impacts on disease progression.
source: Others have similarly shown that cells display a sensitive dependence to initial conditions (in this case, gene expression), and that very small changes in transcriptional regulation and equilibrium may exert potent – perhaps even chaotic – impacts on disease progression (Desi and Tay, 2019; Dorn, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Desi and Tay, 2019; Dorn, 2013.

claim: T-lymphocytes displayed a sharp decline in entropy in the oldest-old group, potentially suggestive of a 'survival effect'.
source: Whereas T-lymphocytes displayed a sharp decline in entropy in the oldest-old group, potentially suggestive of a 'survival effect' (Menichetti et al., 2015), we observed a plateau in entropy after old age (Hayflick, 2007; Menichetti et al., 2015; Samaras, 1974).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Menichetti et al., 2015.

claim: The peak then plateau in entropy may result from a small subset of genes that display highly specific changes from young to old age, followed by a large number of small, non-specific changes between old and oldest-old ages.
source: The data suggest that this peak then plateau may result from a small subset of genes that display highly specific changes from young to old age, followed by a large number of small, non-specific changes between old and oldest-old ages.
evidence: This is an inference based on the entropy data and gene expression data.

claim: The observation that network entropy in mice peaks at old age but that phenotypic changes are not prominent until later in life supports the hypothesis that phenotypic alterations are a lagging indicator of gene expression changes.
source: Our observation that network entropy in mice peaks at old age but that phenotypic changes are not prominent until later in life supports the hypothesis that phenotypic alterations are a lagging indicator of gene expression changes (Frenk and Houseley, 2018).
evidence: This is an inference based on the entropy data and phenotypic data, supported by citation to Frenk and Houseley, 2018.

claim: AAV allows for consistent modulation of Klotho levels without the need for frequent re-administration and without the challenges of recombinant Klotho protein administration.
source: AAV allows for consistent modulation of Klotho levels without the need for frequent re-administration and without the challenges of recombinant Klotho protein administration (Cheikhi et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Cheikhi et al., 2019.

claim: Advanced clinical trials using a similar AAV capsid construct are underway, demonstrating the potential translatability of this method.
source: Advanced clinical trials using a similar capsid construct are underway (George, 2017; Kishnani et al., 2019), demonstrating the potential translatability of this method.
evidence: This is supported by citations to George, 2017; Kishnani et al., 2019.

claim: AAV-Kl administration modulated all hallmarks of aging in old and oldest-old animals, although the magnitude of change was manifold times greater in the oldest-old mice.
source: We found that AAV-Kl administration modulated all hallmarks of aging in old and oldest-old animals, although the magnitude of change was manifold times greater in the oldest-old mice.
evidence: This is supported by differential gene expression analysis shown in Figure 7A,B.

claim: The enhanced response in oldest-old mice was not accompanied by a greater therapeutic benefit.
source: This enhanced response in oldest-old mice was not, however, accompanied by a greater therapeutic benefit.
evidence: This is supported by the functional data shown in Figure 6.

claim: A significant increase in muscle function was observed in old mice receiving AAV-Kl.
source: Instead, though we observed a significant increase in muscle function in old mice receiving AAV-Kl, intervention failed to produce a benefit in the oldest-old mice.
evidence: This is supported by functional data shown in Figure 6H,I.

claim: Intervention failed to produce a benefit in the oldest-old mice.
source: Instead, though we observed a significant increase in muscle function in old mice receiving AAV-Kl, intervention failed to produce a benefit in the oldest-old mice.
evidence: This is supported by functional data shown in Figure 6N,O.

claim: Observations of treatment resistance have been reported in advanced age and critically ill populations in other pharmaceutical treatment studies.
source: Observations of treatment resistance have been reported in advanced age and critically ill populations in other pharmaceutical treatment studies (Rennie, 2009; Burd et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Rennie, 2009; Burd et al., 2013.

claim: In humans, dieting and exercise intervention studies reveal blunted muscle protein synthesis in an older population (greater than 60 years old).
source: In humans, dieting and exercise intervention studies reveal blunted muscle protein synthesis in an older population (greater than 60 years old) (Breen and Phillips, 2011; Durham et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Breen and Phillips, 2011; Durham et al., 2010.

claim: The blunted muscle protein synthesis in older populations coincides with the same stage in which an entropic tipping point was observed.
source: Interestingly, this coincides with the same stage in which we observed a tipping point in network entropy (Figure 3—figure supplement 4C).
evidence: This is an inference based on the entropy data in humans shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4C.

claim: The lack of beneficial response to treatment with increased age is hypothesized to stem from deficiencies in downstream anabolic pathways, that is 'anabolic resistance'.
source: The lack of beneficial response to treatment with increased age is hypothesized to stem from deficiencies in downstream anabolic pathways, that is 'anabolic resistance' (Burd et al., 2013; Glover et al., 2008; Burd et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Burd et al., 2013; Glover et al., 2008; Burd et al., 2012.

claim: Old and oldest-old mice displayed opposing responses to AAV-Kl in pathways associated with cellular structure, lipid membrane integrity, and intercellular communication.
source: Old and oldest-old mice displayed opposing responses to AAV-Kl in pathways associated with cellular structure, lipid membrane integrity, and intercellular communication.
evidence: This is supported by KEGG pathway enrichment analysis shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Cytoskeletal signaling, calcium ion transport (cGMP-PKG signaling), and signaling for muscle adiposity (sphingolipid signaling) displayed biphasic effects in response to Klotho treatment.
source: When we further probed age-dependent pathways that were responsive to Klotho treatment, we found that cytoskeletal signaling, calcium ion transport (cGMP-PKG signaling), and signaling for muscle adiposity (sphingolipid signaling) displayed biphasic effects (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is supported by KEGG pathway enrichment analysis shown in Figure 7D.

claim: The top GO terms for genes that were decreased by Klotho therapy in the old mice are potentially affected by aberrant FGF signaling, including genes associated with calcineurin.
source: Overwhelmingly, the top GO terms for genes that were decreased by Klotho therapy in the old mice are potentially affected by aberrant FGF signaling, including genes associated with calcineurin (Figure 7C, Table 2).
evidence: This is supported by GO term enrichment analysis shown in Figure 7C and Table 2.

claim: Soluble Klotho binds FGF23 to increase its affinity for FGFR1 and prevents its interaction with FGFR4 to reduce expression of the pathogenic calcineurin/NFAT transcriptome.
source: Soluble Klotho binds FGF23 to increase its affinity for FGFR1 and prevents its interaction with FGFR4 to reduce expression of the pathogenic calcineurin/NFAT transcriptome (Ho and Bergwitz, 2021; Han et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ho and Bergwitz, 2021; Han et al., 2020.

claim: FGF23/FGFR4 signaling is associated with muscle pathogenesis in the heart as well as renal fibrosis.
source: Indeed, FGF23/FGFR4 signaling is associated with muscle pathogenesis in the heart as well as renal fibrosis (Han et al., 2020; Hao et al., 2021), processes that, if active in skeletal muscle, could explain the decline in muscle quality over time.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Han et al., 2020; Hao et al., 2021.

claim: If FGF23/FGFR4 signaling is active in skeletal muscle, it could explain the decline in muscle quality over time.
source: Indeed, FGF23/FGFR4 signaling is associated with muscle pathogenesis in the heart as well as renal fibrosis (Han et al., 2020; Hao et al., 2021), processes that, if active in skeletal muscle, could explain the decline in muscle quality over time.
evidence: This is speculation based on the known role of FGF23/FGFR4 signaling in other tissues.

claim: The findings support the hypothesis that restoration of normal calcium signaling and calcineurin/NFAT interactome may be important in the development of therapeutics for sarcopenia.
source: Our findings support the hypothesis that restoration of normal calcium signaling and calcineurin/NFAT interactome may be important in the development of therapeutics for sarcopenia.
evidence: This is an inference based on the pathway analysis and functional data.

claim: Klotho is well-known to regulate calcium signaling and calcineurin/NFAT pathways by promoting interactions with FGF23 and FGFR1.
source: Although Klotho is well-known to regulate these pathways by promoting interactions with FGF23 and FGFR1 (70, 71), the age-dependency of Klotho treatment has not been shown.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of Klotho function.

claim: The age-dependency of Klotho treatment has not been shown.
source: Although Klotho is well-known to regulate these pathways by promoting interactions with FGF23 and FGFR1 (70, 71), the age-dependency of Klotho treatment has not been shown.
evidence: This is a statement about the novelty of the findings in this study.
